implementation_notes: Spring Security inserts one FilterChainProxy ahead of the servlet container; a SecurityFilterChain bean declares the policy (requestMatchers(...).permitAll() plus anyRequest().authenticated()) and the mechanism (formLogin, httpBasic, oauth2ResourceServer) whose AuthenticationManager and providers verify credentials. The filter chain is the enforcer and the providers are the delegated mechanism, so handlers read the Authentication from the SecurityContext instead of authenticating. This is the default realization for Spring Boot stacks; prefer the bare Jakarta API only when the application must stay framework-independent.
pitfalls: The chain only covers servlet-dispatched requests; @Async methods, scheduled jobs and message listeners bypass it and need their own identity propagation.
SecurityContext is thread-bound; asynchronous work loses it unless the context is explicitly propagated (DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor).
Matchers are evaluated in order and the first match wins, so a broad permitAll() placed before a specific authenticated() rule silently opens that path.

variants.name: Jakarta ContainerRequestFilter (framework-independent)
variants.implementation_notes: Without Spring, the checkpoint is the raw Jakarta API: a servlet Filter mapped by URL pattern, or a JAX-RS ContainerRequestFilter bound to resources with a @NameBinding annotation, which runs before the resource method, delegates verification to a token verifier or JAAS, and either aborts with requestContext.abortWith(Response.status(401)) or sets the SecurityContext. Resources are protected exactly when annotated, so annotation coverage is the policy. Use it to stay framework-independent; Spring Security remains the better default when Spring Boot already forms the stack.
pitfalls: A @NameBinding filter only executes for annotated resources; every unannotated endpoint is silently public, so the annotation coverage is the security policy and must be reviewed.
Store the subject with ctx.setSecurityContext; writing it into a static field or a shared request attribute leaks identities when the container reuses threads.
